pages.title: Constitutionalism as Strategy and Gokhale's Definition
pages.summary: Constitutionalism as a strategy is rooted in liberalism's belief that rational human beings can resolve conflicts through dialogue without street politics or violence. Gokhale defined constitutional methods as seeking changes through constituted authorities via assembly resolutions, memorials, and prayers.

pages.title: Early Nationalists' Adoption of Constitutional Methods
pages.summary: Constitutional methods exclude direct actions such as satyagraha, non-cooperation, boycotts, and rebellion. Influenced by liberalism, early nationalists like Ranade, Banerjee, and Naoroji viewed British rule as a divine blessing bringing justice and the rule of law.

pages.title: Historical Reasons and Criticisms of Constitutional Methods
pages.summary: Leaders like Gokhale, Chintamani, and Bipin Chandra noted that direct action was historically premature due to disunity and a lack of subjective consciousness among the masses. Critics including Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh, and Nehru condemned constitutional methods under an alien bureaucracy as political suicide and intellectual bankruptcy.

pages.title: Bipin Chandra's Assessment and Rise of Extremists
pages.summary: Bipin Chandra noted that moderates laid the ideological foundation for mass movement despite frequent failures. The extremist phase emerged with leaders like Lal, Bal, and Pal, who favored direct action and differed from moderates mainly on the pace of political reform.

pages.title: Rise, Methods, and Evaluation of Extremists
pages.summary: Extremists rejected petitioning and favored direct action, with Tilak asserting swaraj as a birthright and justifying resistance against exploitative British governance. The rise of extremists was driven by lack of moderate achievements, rollbacks like the Calcutta Corporation Act, famines, and the Partition of Bengal.

pages.title: Unique Features of Gandhian Mass Movements
pages.summary: Bipin Chandra characterizes the Indian National Movement as a unique, spectacular, and controlled mass movement reaching its logical end. Unlike overnight revolutions, the Gandhian struggle was a protracted fight operating through both the War of Position and the War of Maneuver.

pages.title: Two-Stage Revolution and Gandhian Struggle Strategy
pages.summary: A two-stage revolution was needed to reveal the true exploitative character of British rule and respect the limited capacity of the masses. Gandhi proactively alternated between active struggle and passive phases of constructive programmes, known as the struggle-truce-struggle strategy.

pages.title: Non-Cooperation Movement Causes, Strategy, and Programme
pages.summary: The Non-Cooperation Movement emerged from grievances including the Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh tragedy, economic distress, and the Khilafat issue. Approved at the 1920 Nagpur session to attain swaraj within a year, its programme included title surrenders, boycotts, and an optional no-tax campaign.

pages.title: Non-Cooperation Programme Details and Chauri-Chaura Withdrawal
pages.summary: The movement promoted national schools, panchayat courts, khadi, and unity through peaceful and legitimate means rather than constitutional ones. Gandhi abruptly ended the movement after the Chauri-Chaura incident, which Bipin Chandra analyzes as a graceful exit due to mass exhaustion, eroding Hindu-Muslim solidarity, and impending government retaliation.

pages.title: Assessment of the Non-Cooperation Movement
pages.summary: Although the movement failed to achieve swaraj within a year, it successfully tested mass capacity and proved Congress represented a multi-class mass movement. Visible achievements included burning foreign clothes and boycotting the visit of the Prince of Wales.

pages.title: Civil Disobedience Movement: Nature, Reasons, and Demands
pages.summary: The Civil Disobedience Movement represented a direct challenge to government authority and laws, influenced by Thoreau's concept of peaceful protest against unjust laws. Due to rising anti-British sentiment from the Simon Commission, Lala Lajpat Rai's death, and economic depression, Gandhi presented eleven demands including abolishing the salt tax.

pages.title: Gandhi's Strategy and Quit India Movement Introduction
pages.summary: Gandhi's offensive strategy placed the government in a dilemma, leading to the 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact where most demands were accepted and Congress gained equal footing. The 1942 Quit India Movement began as Gandhi's most militant and ungandhian campaign, demanding the British quit India and permitting armed self-defence against aggressors.

pages.title: Quit India Movement Features and Strategic Violence
pages.summary: During Quit India, Gandhi called for 'do or die', refused to condemn public violence or halt the movement, and permitted taking control of police stations. According to Francis Hutchins, Gandhi was a politician and strategist who used non-violence to mobilize the masses, discarding it once they joined the national movement.

pages.title: Quit India Responses and the Revolutionary Movement
pages.summary: Various leaders and groups opposed the Quit India Movement, including Ambedkar, the Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, and C. Rajagopalachari. In contrast to terrorists who target civilians, revolutionaries used violence against oppressors and drew inspiration from texts like Anandmath and Nihilists to awaken patriotic sentiments.

pages.title: Revolutionary Impact and Peasant Movements Phase I
pages.summary: After noting that revolutionaries removed fear of authority and displayed heroism, the page outlines how British land settlement policies provoked peasant revolts like the 1860 Indigo revolt. In the 1920s first phase, Gandhi adopted a conciliatory approach to peasant concerns, in contrast to the protest-oriented communist approach.

pages.title: Peasant Movement Phases II, III, and Assessment
pages.summary: In the 1930s and 1940s, peasant movements organized under the All India Kisan Sabha and later communist-dominated struggles like Tebhaga and Telangana demanding land reforms. Overall, peasant movements failed to achieve concrete gains due to caste and religious divisions, leaving land reforms unfinished and giving rise to Maoist extremism.

pages.title: Trade Union Movement: Characteristics and Chronology
pages.summary: The trade union movement in India has historically remained weak, divided along caste and religious lines, and subordinated to political parties without developing autonomy. The chronology spans late 19th-century worker emergence, early philanthropic leadership, the formation of AITUC in 1920, and shifting communist splits leading to INTUC.

flashcards.front: How did Gopal Krishna Gokhale define constitutional methods at the 1907 Allahabad Congress session?
flashcards.back: Gokhale defined constitutional methods as actions seeking desired changes through constituted authorities, such as bringing resolutions in assemblies, sending memorials, prayers, petitions, and appeals to justice. These methods strictly excluded direct mass action, passive resistance, boycotts, and violent rebellion.

flashcards.front: What ideological beliefs led early nationalists to view British rule as a blessing in disguise?
flashcards.back: Influenced by liberalism, early nationalists viewed British rule as divine intervention to eradicate past misrule. Ranade praised the introduction of the rule of law, Banerjee sought institutions truly British in character, and Dadabhai Naoroji trusted the British to be justice-loving people.

flashcards.front: Why did early nationalists consider direct mass action inappropriate according to Gokhale, Chintamani, and Bipan Chandra?
flashcards.back: Gokhale argued direct action required immense preparation, while C.Y. Chintamani stressed addressing internal divisions first. Bipan Chandra noted that while objective colonial conditions united Indians, the necessary subjective consciousness was still developing among leaders and masses.

flashcards.front: On what grounds did Tilak, Aurobindo Ghosh, and Nehru criticize moderate constitutionalism?
flashcards.back: Tilak argued that constitutionalism before an alien bureaucracy was political suicide because India lacked a constitutional government. Aurobindo Ghosh condemned constitutional methods as the intellectual bankruptcy of moderates, while Jawaharlal Nehru asserted constitutional methods were impossible without constitutional governance.

flashcards.front: What underlying causes precipitated the emergence of militant extremist nationalism within Congress?
flashcards.back: Extremism arose due to the lack of concrete moderate achievements, government rollback of reforms via the Calcutta Corporation Act 1899 and Indian Universities Act 1904, and official apathy during famines and epidemics. The Partition of Bengal dealt the final blow, leading Congress to adopt Swadeshi.

flashcards.front: How does Bipan Chandra explain Mahatma Gandhi's Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S) strategy?
flashcards.back: Bipan Chandra observed that Gandhi recognized the limited capacity of masses for sustained confrontation, alternating active struggle with passive truce. During truce phases, Gandhi pursued constructive programmes and consolidated strength, ensuring movements remained proactive rather than reactive.

flashcards.front: Why did Gandhi abruptly terminate the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 according to Bipan Chandra?
flashcards.back: Following the Chauri Chaura incident, Gandhi sought a graceful exit because the masses were tiring, Hindu-Muslim solidarity was fraying after the Mappila revolt, and imminent state retaliation threatened future mobilization. Calling off the movement prevented these internal weaknesses from being exposed.

flashcards.front: How did the Civil Disobedience Movement's strategy put the colonial government in a dilemma?
flashcards.back: If the government used force against non-violent protesters defying salt laws, it exploded the myth of benevolent despotism, whereas not using force surrendered authority to direct challenge. Delayed repression enabled Gandhi to complete the Salt March, igniting nationwide protests.

flashcards.front: What distinct ideological and tactical features made the 1942 Quit India Movement un-Gandhian?
flashcards.back: Gandhi demanded the British Quit India rather than merely fighting systemic evil, issued the 'Do or Die' call, permitted armed self-defence, and sanctioned seizing police stations. Furthermore, he refused to condemn popular violence and declared he would not call off the struggle.

flashcards.front: How does the notes distinguish between revolutionary nationalists and terrorists in their methods and targets?
flashcards.back: Revolutionaries directed violence specifically against oppressors and state authorities to awaken national consciousness and display heroism. In contrast, terrorists resort to indiscriminate violence against civilians and innocent individuals to create terror.

answers.question: Critically examine the constitutional methods adopted by early nationalists. Was constitutionalism a political miscalculation or an objective historical necessity?
answers.intro: Early nationalists adopted constitutionalism rooted in liberalism, believing rational dialogue with constituted authorities could resolve conflicts. While critics derided this as passive mendicancy, moderates laid the vital ideological foundation for India's subsequent anti-colonial mass struggle.
body: Gopal Krishna Gokhale defined constitutional methods as working through constituted authorities via memorials, petitions, and assembly resolutions. Mahadev Govind Ranade and Surendranath Banerjee viewed British rule as a divine dispensation introducing rule of law, while Dadabhai Naoroji argued reasonable appeals would persuade a justice-loving British public.

Direct mass action was historically premature. Gokhale stressed that direct action required immense preparation, whereas C.Y. Chintamani highlighted prevailing internal divisions. Bipan Chandra notes that while colonial rule created objective unities, subjective national consciousness was nascent, making moderates both pioneering leaders and learners.

Extremist thinkers severely criticized this gradualism. Bal Gangadhar Tilak declared constitutionalism before an alien bureaucracy political suicide and advocated Praja Droh. Aurobindo Ghosh termed it intellectual bankruptcy, and Jawaharlal Nehru maintained that constitutional methods were impossible without constitutional governance.

Despite legislative reversals like the Calcutta Corporation Act 1899 and Indian Universities Act 1904, Bipan Chandra observes that moderates successfully exposed colonial economic exploitation. Ranade clarified that petitions were truly addressed to educate Indians, building national resilience through initial failures.
answers.conclusion: Constitutionalism was not mere naivety but an indispensable developmental phase. As Gokhale presciently noted, early failures nurtured national strength, providing the institutional vocabulary and ideological critique that enabled Tilak and Gandhi to mobilize future mass movements.

answers.question: Critically examine whether the Quit India Movement of 1942 was the 'most un-Gandhian of all Gandhian movements'. How does it reflect Gandhi's evolving political strategy?
answers.topic: Quit India Movement and Gandhian Strategy
answers.intro: The 1942 Quit India Movement departed from earlier Gandhian struggles through its militancy, spontaneity, and tolerance of violence. Rather than an ideological rupture, it marked the tactical climax of Gandhi's protracted war of movement against British colonialism.
body: Unlike the Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements, Gandhi shifted focus from fighting systemic evil to demanding that the evil-doer immediately Quit India. Adopting the uncompromising slogan 'Do or Die', he declared this his final struggle and refused to call off the campaign.

Departing from rigid non-violence, Gandhi permitted arms in self-defence against aggressors, authorized seizing police stations, and refused to condemn public violence, terming it a natural reaction to state brutality. Congress prescribed no procedural restrictions, urging activists to defend themselves rather than passively endure blows.

Historian Francis Hutchins interprets Gandhi as a consummate strategist who utilized non-violence instrumentally to draw masses into political action, discarding strict non-violence once mass mobilization matured. Bipan Chandra categorizes this as Gandhi's decisive war of movement following a protracted war of position.

The agitation provoked intense contemporary opposition: B.R. Ambedkar condemned it as a mad venture, C. Rajagopalachari feared widespread anarchy, while the Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha opposed it. Yet, grassroots leadership spontaneously led the revolt after senior leaders were jailed.
answers.conclusion: Quit India was un-Gandhian in method but quintessentially Gandhian in objective. By transforming the masses into self-directed leaders, Gandhi demonstrated strategic flexibility, proving that non-violent discipline could transition into decisive assertiveness when colonial legitimacy had completely collapsed.
